title: I don't want the details
author: mooreds
tldr: After an incident, asking why it happened tends to produce a reasonable story and no change. Michael Heap, retelling how an SVP cut off his explanation, argues the useful question is what the team will change so the same class of failure gets less likely.

keyPoints: When Heap started explaining a failure, his SVP of engineering stopped him. The reasons would be perfectly reasonable, the SVP said, everyone would empathise, and then it would happen again, so he wanted to hear what was changing.
Heap first took this as dismissive, then read it as trust. The SVP assumed the people involved were competent and wanted to skip straight to what happens next.
A good explanation can make things worse. Once everyone agrees the behaviour was reasonable, nobody feels urgency to change anything, and the same incident returns six months later.
Postmortem actions like "communicate better" or "be more careful" are hopes, not fixes. His test is whether the fix would still work if everyone involved left the company tomorrow.
Not every failure deserves a new process. Accepting a risk is fine when the team decides it on purpose, which is different from promising to try harder.
article.whyItMatters: It's a four-minute read, and the summary covers nearly all of it. Open the original for the three example excuses paired with the system question each one should prompt, which work as a checklist for reviewing your own postmortem action items.

comments.overview: Most of the thread pushed back hard. The main objection was that a leader can't judge whether a fix is any good without hearing what broke, and a good share of commenters read the SVP as dismissive or as dodging accountability. Defenders argued that an SVP's job is resourcing and coordination, not the technical replay, and a steady minority dismissed the post as LinkedIn-style or AI-sounding writing.

themes.title: You can't evaluate a fix without the problem
themes.synthesis: The largest camp said the details are what tell you whether a proposed change fits the failure. The Alice-and-Bob example in the article is itself the details, one commenter noted, and teams working in silos often propose changes that don't hold together across the organization. Defenders replied that the team still does the root-cause work; the SVP just doesn't need to sit through it. Several asked what the SVP was in the meeting for if they wouldn't engage.

quotes.author: rpdillon
quotes.text: I don't like approaches that proxy "I understand the problem" with "I have a solution", and saying I trust someone doesn't cover this; it's firmly in the "trust but verify" category.

quotes.author: tristor
quotes.text: The executive is there to help with the big picture, but you can't see the big picture if the canvas is blank.

themes.title: What trust buys a leader, and what the SVP is for
themes.synthesis: The top thread opened with a dilemma. If you fully trust the team you don't need the plan either, and if you don't, you can't judge the plan without the details. Replies pulled "trust" apart: trusting that people acted reasonably is different from trusting them to fix things alone. Others listed concrete reasons an executive wants the plan but not the timeline: reporting upward, freeing budget or headcount, spotting conflicts with other teams' work. One commenter added that leaders who absorb every detail cap how many teams the organization can run.

quotes.author: dpark
quotes.text: Trusting that people are capable and well intentioned does not mean trusting that they will accomplish the same thing without you.

quotes.author: unregistereddev
quotes.text: The SVP is inviting a higher level discussion around what resources need to be consumed in order to be sure this doesn't happen again. And they're opening the door to defending that use of resources.

themes.title: Efficient or dismissive
themes.synthesis: Even commenters who liked the SVP's point thought the wording was poor, since "I don't want the details" lands as "don't waste my time" and wears on morale. Harsher readings called it a power move, a refusal to hear people out, or a way to shift risk downward, where "we" are changing something but you own the decision. A few defended bluntness as respect for everyone's time.

quotes.author: dofm
quotes.text: But otherwise be very wary of this pattern of communication where "we" might mean "you".

quotes.author: cushychicken
quotes.text: My claim is that it would have taken slightly more words to get that point across without any reputational downside to the SVP.

themes.title: Why versus what is a false choice
themes.synthesis: Many said every postmortem they have done already ends in action items, so the article attacks a straw man, and the "why" is what tells you what to change. Others went after root-cause analysis itself. Complex failures have many contributing factors, and a team forced to find one root cause will produce one. A CAPA story showed the opposite failure, where a plain typo got pushed up into a form-design flaw because human error wasn't an acceptable root cause.

quotes.author: scsh
quotes.text: "How/why did this happen?" informs how you answer "What are we changing?"

quotes.author: juancn
quotes.text: My other nit with these is a term that's abused a lot "Root Cause", most complex issues have many contributing factors, not a single root cause, and if you force the teams to find one, they will.

themes.title: Changes cost something, and action items rot
themes.synthesis: Some faulted the SVP's question for leaving out the cost of the change. Fixes compete for time and money, and for a minor incident the right answer may be no change, which the article concedes only in its last section. Others said improvement processes only ever add rules and checks until work slows to a crawl. And the action items that do get written often sit in a backlog nobody gets to.

quotes.author: kevin_nisbet
quotes.text: And then even should changes be part of the outcomes, how expensive are those to implement compared to whatever the issue was, and if they're too expensive compared to the risk, don't put resources into it.

quotes.author: Pxtl
quotes.text: Actionable items go onto the backlog.  The backlog grows from the top.

comments.consensus: Postmortems should end in concrete changes to the system rather than promises to be careful, and an executive doesn't need a minute-by-minute replay. The article's line about "organizational folklore" drew praise even from its critics.
comments.dissent: Most commenters rejected the idea that "why" and "what changes" are separate questions. In their view a leader who won't hear the problem can't judge the fix, and the SVP's framing, intended or not, came across as dismissive or as pushing risk onto subordinates.

contrarian.author: btilly
contrarian.text: The leader in this case trusted the technical person to produce an accurate description of what happened. But didn't trust that same person to arrive at a solution that met the business of having a similar disaster not happen the next time.
contrarian.why: Both the article and its critics treat the exchange as a vote of trust, but this reads it as partial distrust delivered politely, which explains the SVP's behavior better than either.
